ACKNOWLEDGMENT BY LADY ABERDEEN OF MESSAGE OF SYMPATHY FROM HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I have a communication
to make to the house. Pursuant to your wishes I conveyed to Lady Aberdeen the
sympathy of the house expressed in this chamber on the passing of her husband, the late Lord Aberdeen, former Governor General of Canada, and have received from her the following reply:
House of Cromar,
Tarland, Aberdeenshire,
April 3, 1934.
Dear Mr. Speaker:
I beg you to accept yourself and to convey to the members of the Canadian House of Commons the most grateful thanks of my family and myself for the message of understanding sympathy which you have been good enough to convey to me on their behalf.
We are very sensible of the high honour paid to my late husband by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition and the leader of the Progressive party, all speaking so appreciatively of Lord Aberdeen's character and career, and I only wish he could himself have read the report of their speeches and heard of the unanimous resolution passed. He had a very deep love for Canada and it would indeed have been a joy to him to know that he was thus remembered by the House of Commons.
I can only beg you to believe that Lord Aberdeen's family and' friends do most keenly appreciate this signal mark of honour and affection.
Yours very sincerely,
Ishbel Aberdeen and Temair.

The matter to which the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska refers is one which has been brought to the attention of the government from many sources. For instance, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) at present beside me has been pressing the matter upon our attention and members for the Essex constituencies as well as those concerned who live in western constituencies bordering on the United States have also been bringing the matter to our notice. The legislation that has been introduced into congress is similar in terms to legislation that has frequently been introduced there. It has not, however, been enacted heretofore. Whether the present legislation will or will not be enacted is something about which it is impossible for the government to make a statement. There are large numbers of people living in Canada who work in the United States and likewise there are large numbers of people who live in the United

States who work in Canada. Heretofore the spirit of good neighbourliness that has characterized the relations between the two countries and to which the president made reference a few days ago has enabled those who live in Canada to cross the border from day to day to work in the United States and those who live in the United States to cross the border from day to day to work in Canada. The government has, of course, taken notice of the legislation and through the appropriate channels made to the United States authorities such representations as were thought desirable. It will be time enough to determine what action should be taken by Canada should the legislation to which the hon. member refers become law. I can make no further statement than I have just made with respect to the matter except to assure the hon. member and all those who are concerned, that the government is fully seized of the seriousness of the situation and has made to the United States government as strong representations as are possible under the circumstances.

The shouts of order remind me of something that comes to us from across the boundary, of negro spirituals. The preacher starts to say something, then he gets enthused and the audience shouts the louder with ham and then someone faints or drops outside the church and they restore him with buckets of water. That is what should be done to those who are so noisy on the other side of the house.
But, sir, this is a serious business. The government have been trading in wheat and steel, and so on. I wonder why the government offices are not transferred to the market square. There are two or three days in the week for marketing. I would like to deal with those gentlemen, I wonder if they would be disposed to give credit to an individual, I would like to be as well connected with them as the Algoma Steel Corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway and Mr. McFarland. However, leaving negro spirituals, let us come to the blank cheque. What I do not understand in that legislation is the mystery of it. Everything is done in the fashion of the magic rope in India. The fakir burns some wood, there is a cloud of smoke, then the rope hangs straight up in the cloud and he does all sorts of magic in that cloud of smoke.
Will the government follow the wonderful example of the Hindoo fakir. Some small
Relief Act, 1934

guarantees have been given by the government, in the name of the country at large, to the steel corporations in Ontario and Nova Scotia as well as to other corporations, but this is what I find most extraordinary. We heard a great deal from hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to Beauharnois; they found it a very bad proposition, and they destroyed the credit of that corporation. Then, after having done so, they supplied it with crutches to the extent of $15,000,000, by way of guarantee.
Unfortunately I have not the gift of ubiquity; yesterday I was unable to be in the house because I was attending the meetings of a committee, so I did not have an opportunity of listening to the debate. On reading Hansard this morning, however, I was delighted to see how hon. gentlemen on this side of the house pointed out the absurdity of this legislation. I should like to compliment all who took part in that debate, but I would particularly mention my good friend from Antigonish-Guysborough. First he spoke with a smile; then he brought facts to the house to which there was no answer. It is sad not to receive an answer when such important matters are discussed, but after reading what took place yesterday may I say that I fully agree with the well founded remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough who asked that the government guarantee loans to the fishermen of his constituency to the extent of $15,000. The right hon. Prime Minister thought the hon. member was not perhaps a happy medium. Medium is another word that is used in connection with spiritualism, but it is just a word, like protoplasm. A member is not a magician; a member cannot make bad things look good, as the government attempts to do. It is our duty to secure from the government information which we supply to our constituents, and that information must be accurate. The member elected from each constituency is the connecting link between that constituency and the government. Very often the suggestions that come from this side of the house are disregarded by the government; the government have that power, but when they take the trouble to consider the real needs of the nation they are forced to admit that the members on this side of the house, who do not pretend to be infallible, are earnest in their desire to promote the welfare of our country.
I am not surprised, sir, that my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough was unsuccessful in presenting the request of his electors to the government, because I know that some 
requests that have been made to the federal government by the provincial government of Quebec have been disregarded. The other day I mentioned the case of the poor settlers of Saint-Emile d'Auclair, Saint-Elzear and Packington. An inspector was sent to those parishes by the department, and he made a report saying that those people should not have the relief works asked for by the Quebec government. After a further investigation, however, and after the parish priest had come to the government with tears in his eyes and described the real condition of those poor people, the eyes and heart of the Minister of Labour were opened. In other places, however, the government did not reconsider its decision and did not approve of the relief works which had been asked for by the Quebec government, What was the explanation given by the government? He stated that in connection with the last two parishes they had received a list of the unemployed in a letter which bore no date or signature and which did not contain a covering letter, but that the department had a confidential report from the inspector in this connection. If the report was confidential in regard to the members of the opposition it was not in any way confidential in regard to the minister, because it came to him from one of his employees. The minister should have looked into the matter; he should have paid attention to it. He should have sent reliable men as inspectors, who would give him a true picture of the situation. I have received tens and hundreds of letters from those people complaining of their dire distress, and I wonder how it is possible for the poor people of this country, who have not an opportunity to present their case to the government, to be heard by hon. gentlemen opposite.
I have often told the government that they are wrongly informed, that they obtain their information from interested parties. Those who could tell the true facts are not those who flatter; they are those who stand silent. Those who come to the government are those who flatter in an endeavour to obtain something from the government, and they paint false pictures of the conditions that exist. They deceive the government for their own benefit. This is being done now, and this is why I complain so much. I regret that wihen we do our duty as defenders of the rights and privileges of these poor people we can get no answer from the government. The report is called confidential, and it must be a contagious confidence which spreads like a disease because every paper filed next to such confidential report of an inspector is also

called confidential. The word "confidential" is spread through the whole file, and it is impossible to get any information. I have said very often in this House of Commons, and I shall now repeat, that I will not accuse any hon. member of the government of having a stone where in the normal human body we find a heart. I believe they are generous. They are good natured and average men. I regret however that they are wrongly informed, and at times I am sure they are afraid to face the facts. They act like a man who is condemned to death because of illness, a man who is afraid to see his doctor for fear he will be told, "My friend draw up your will; you will die within a few hours." The government is afraid of that and they will not listen to those who are their good friends and who are willing to tell them when they are mistaken, and give them a chance to change their policy.
The stand I now take is not taken selfishly, but is taken on behalf of my people. Unfortunately however those who take that stand are found only on this side of the house. I regret very much that the case of those settlers has not been considered by the government.

I shall not insist upon an answer to what I have said about the settlers, because I know I shall receive none. However as the Prime Minister was good enough to supply me with a copy of the Amulree report I shall ask him if the Canadian government has been released from the guarantees given to Newfoundland, and if following that release Canada will have anything to say in the future for the guarantee which has been given to the banks on behalf of Newfoundland. I appeal to the members of this committee, those who know and understand what happened, who know that the government left it a perfectly open question for the members to determine as they saw fit, and that the committee decided as it did in the light of the knowledge they had as to what was best for the country under the circumstances. It is little credit to any hon. member to raise that issue in the way in which they have endeavoured to raise it in this case. Of course the west has had large benefits from the relief measures. Why? Because there we have a small number of people inhabiting a vast area, who produced more wealth per capita for Canada than any pioneer people in the world. That is the real truth, if you want to know the real truth. Everyone who takes the trouble to analyze the statistics realizes the great amount of new wealth that has been produced on the western plains between the head of the lakes and the mountains during the last ten years; new wealth coming into being year by year, not baking five or Bix years to produce but produced between the spring and the fall, which had such a tremendous effect on this country that now the drying up of this source of production has been felt in every part of this dominion. I want to say a few words before this amendment carries. I do not want to be too long because hon. gentlemen to your right, Mr. Chairman, would try to lead the house and the country to believe that we are intentionally trying to delay the passage of this legislation which is coming to the rescue of the needy. The Prime Minister a few minutes ago, replying to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, said that we on this aide of the house were opposed to relief and t.o whatever has been done for the western provinces; he said that we wanted to raise prejudices and to divide east from west. As no one has answered this implication, which is absolutely wrong, may I be allowed to say for n^self and, if I may do so, in the name of the province from which I come, that we from the province of Quebec are always glad to see this government come to the rescue of the western provinces, and have always approved of what has been done in that regard. As far as I can recollect we have never objected in this house to any legislation intended to assist the needy in the west, but we do object to having two ways of doing it. We object to two measures. The Prime Minister raised his voice in protest against an interruption of mine in regard to Montreal. He said, "We received only yesterday the report from the Montreal relief people." May I say to him, with all due respect, that he is not in a position to say that we are responsible for any delays in administration, in bookkeeping in the large centres of Canada.
What I intended to say on behalf of Montreal and of the eastern provinces was this. What we want is an opportunity to work, not to beg our bread as direct relief compels the people to do. The people want work, and if I said that enough had not been done for Montreal I had in mind the fact that prior to 1930 the Liberal government had voted 850.000,000 to build a central station in Montreal, and that as soon as this government came into powrer, owing to the advice, not of representatives of the west, not of the mayor of Toronto or of the mayor of Vancouver, but on the advice of a revengeful citizen of Montreal, who was then mayor of that city, this government stopped the spending of this 850,000,000 for the construction of that central station, which would have given work to hundreds, yes, thousands of people in

Montreal who are now starving. There are works of different kinds that might have been done in Montreal, and help in other directions might have been given to our province and other eastern provinces, which this government has not carried out. That is all we are complaining about, and I say that the Prime Minister has no right to take advantage of a situation like this to make political capital out of it, if I may use his words, and to try to say to the western people, "You see the Liberal opposition from the eastern provinces are angry at my government for having come to the rescue of you people in the west." He has no right to take this attitude and I protest very strongly against it; he should give us justice. We may be very small in his eyes, but we are the representatives of the people, and we come from a province the intentions of the people of which are, to say the least, just as good as those of the right hon. representative of Calgary.
The Prime Minister also complains that we are intentionally delaying this legislation. As far as that goes, I fully concur in what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has said. VTe support this bill, but we contend that it places in the hands of the government very drastic powers. Let me ask the government this question. If they are so anxious to help the needy and the unemployed, and knowing as they do that we object to the provision with respect to peace, order and good government, and have objected to it for the past four years, then they cannot plead ignorance of our attitude to this legislation so far as that particular provision is concerned. That being so, may I ask the Prime Minister why this bill was not introduced earlier in the session. Mind you, that was a very pressing piece of legislation, apparently, from his point of view, so pressing that the government did not want to wait a single day to have it passed. I just want to conclude this question by saying that when I spoke of equal justice I did not have in mind any undue delays on the part of his government with regard to direct relief; I had in mind what I have already stated-help to the unemployed, and in divers fields of activities and forms. May I say that in our province of Quebec, and perhaps I shall not be wrong if I say in Ontario also, the situation of the farmers is in some cases just as bad as that of our friends in the west. But nothing has been done for the Quebec people, although during the last election promises were made *that paradise on earth should come to us. I hate to recall those promises, but the farmers of Quebec are in such need that they are just as much entitled to help as our friends in the west, yet nothing has been done for them. That is what I was saying a few moments ago; we want equal justice. The credit of our farmers is absolutely destroyed; their products remain unsold on their farms. I will not discuss the tariff question now; I just state the situation as it is. Farm after farm is being sold by the sheriff or abandoned, yet our farmers could have been rescued or 'helped by this government-there is no excuse for this government not helping them by a guarantee in some way or another of their mortgages. But nothing has been done. The farm loan board created by this parliament to lend money to the farmer offers unacceptable conditions, and a rate so high that the farmers cannot take advantage of it. This government knew when they came into power that they must do something for the farmers, and not only the western farmers. I repeat that I am not jealous of what the government has done for the west; they were right in doing it; it was good policy to help them in the difficulties they were facing owing to the decline in the export market for wheat. With respect to one advance no interest was charged, nor was interest to be charged; the principal was to be repaid. This was done instead of carrying on relief, and the amount saved, anticipating that the principal would be repaid in a reasonable time, is considerable as against paying direct relief to the number of people involved. The second loan bears interest and is repayable when the Canadian Pacific is in a position to pay it which, under present conditions, would seem to be reasonably within sight.
The provinces all have agreed to pay interest. The advances are evidenced by treasury bills. At first the rate was 5i per cent; then it was 5 per cent, and I am not sure that it is not a little lower now. There is no security on a treasury bill given the dominion, any more than there is with respect to a treasury bill given by the dominion or by any province. My first word will be to congratulate the minister on retaining the grant to the horticultural council. I am not even going to ask him why he has retained that grant and eliminated the one to the national dairy council, but possibly he will give us a synopsis of what the situation is on the western fruit front, the eastern fruit front and the central fruit front, with regard to pests. Have new insect pests been infecting the fruit of the country and have old ones been surmounted? Any news of interest to the committee will be welcome, and if the minister will give us this information it may save a lot of questions. He might also tell
fMr. Motherwell.]
us whether there is any danger looming up in the offing of the likelihood of the British government applying a quota to our apples or other fruit. If the minister would start with that he could then glide on to the other question with regard to the pest situation, and the quality standing of our fruit. I am also interested in how he is getting on with the inspectional work in the maritimes, which was not an easy matter at the start. Under his administration it has been considerably improved I understand. Shipping point inspection has always been sound, and while the maritimes took it up reluctantly I think it has made great progress.

There has been no official
intimation that any restriction will be placed upon the shipment of our fruit to the United Kingdom, and no new injurious insects have made their appearance during the past year. Perhaps in this connection the most important work has been that done in Ontario and Nova Scotia through the formation of combined advisory committees-that is, committees formed by officials in the provincial departments together with the officials in the federal department and those outside either department-to make a survey and decide the best plan of action to reduce infestation by the apple maggot. Both provinces have been one hundred per cent behind this campaign, and the results of the campaign in both Nova Scotia and Ontario have been, I am very glad to say, much more satisfactory than even the most optimistic expected in view of the very great infestation that has taken place in the provinces affected.
As the hon. member for Melville stated, there has been cooperation between the government of Nova Scotia and the federal government with respect to orchard inspection for apple maggot infestation, which for some time had caused a good deal of concern and irritation. There is now enforced shipping point inspection for apples for export, and the fruit growers are fully alive to the necessity of enforced and rigorous inspection of all kinds, especially in connection with fruit for export.

I suggest to my hon. friend that until we can get outside inspectors to do the inspection in these various districts, including the maritimes, we shall always have some difficulty in getting exact and reliable inspection. Whether it be in regard to school inspectors, or bank inspectors or railway agents, the head men of each such institution usually find it advisable to change

Supply-A griculture-Frui t
inspectors around. During my experience with the maritimes, and with other places as well but particularly the maritimes, I found that they were intensely wedded to the idea of local inspectors for each constituency, and it was almost a sacrilege to suggest that anyone outside should come in and inspect apples -I am speaking of about ten years ago. I was glad to note some betterment, though not to the extent that I should like to have seen. Local influences are very strong in support of having local men, and so long as that continues it will be very difficult to obtain proper inspection of fruit, because of the tendency to be a little easy with neighbours. That however can be overcome very largely when they get it into their heads that the certificate of the government behind any product must be lived up to or it is not worth the paper it is written on. In the early days our wheat certificates had not the value they acquired later on. Of course, the certificates always had a fair value, but they must have a proven value, backed by a number of years' experience on the part of buyers, and once the buyers are fully confident that the certificates are bona fide and that the article in question is up to the standard certified to, the certificate is of inestimable value in selling the product. I am not saying that the maritimes are worse than others in this prospect anywhere else, but they have not become quite familiar with the idea and advantage of outside inspectors. A consignment of potatoes and apples was once shipped up to the old fruit branch building here and examined-the fruit commissioner sitting in front of the minister will recall the time- and when the barrels were opened and inspected, it was a holy terror, what they contained. That day, I hope, has gone by, and if the inspection is further tightened up there will not be a recurrence of such an experience.
In 1928 I was at Covent Garden in London, the most wonderful horticultural market I have ever seen, and they knew much more about Canadian apples than I did. They knew all about the British Columbia apples and about the determination of the fruit growers there to live up to standard. They also spoke highly of the Ontario apple and were delighted also with the maritime apples, as to quality, which could not be better; but, oh dear, they were disappointed about the packing, and those buyers stated candidly they wanted to know what was in the barrels before they would do any bidding on them in the auction rooms.
I am speaking candidly but I hope not harshly; but unless the inspection of fruit is followed up continuously and outside inspection employed the ones who are putting up a good pack are disposed to become indifferent if the others are not doing the same.
I make these suggestions believing that great progress is being made, but it should be accelerated, because in this day of overabundance it is becoming harder and harder to sell a poor product, while on the other hand there is always a great advantage in selling a good product, because it helps greatly to sell itself.

What the hon. member has said is very true about local pressure being brought to bear upon inspectors who are appointed locally. I believe what has had a good deal to do with the change in attitude in this connection has been realization on the part of fruit growers of the importance, especially in connection with export, of a very thorough and rigid inspection. In Nova Scotia in particular a very definite effort is being made to improve the quality of the pack with especially good results. As the hon. member has said, one of the chief criticisms of Nova Scotia apples for export has been in connection with the quality of the pack. In view of what has been said and of the difficulty in many cases in the work of inspection, it would be interesting to the committee to receive a condensed summary of the inspections. In the whole dominion during the past year the paid inspections numbered 26,681, the reinspections asked for numbering 245, or a percentage of all inspections of .92 per cent. After reinspection by other inspectors reversals in certificates were only 16 or a percentage of the total inspections of .06, which I think is the finest compliment we can pay to the thoroughness of the work of our fruit inspectors.

Is there a charge for that
inspection?

Why should there be a
charge for the inspection of fruit when as regards almost every other commodity such as meat, bacon and so on, the inspections are given free of charge? It has always been a wonder to me why there should be this charge for fruit inspections.

The reason for the charge for fruit inspection is that it was at first instituted at the request of the growers themselves and it has been continued or extended from time to tamei, at the request of the industry. There are other products the inspection of which has to be paid for; grains, grass seeds, hay, turnips, potatoes, grapes,

Personally, I feel the tendency is toward paid inspection for all these products, the industry feeling that if they pay they will have a better claim to ask for further and more specific inspection for the commodity as they realize the importance of the inspectional work.

Why should that not
apply to meat inspection in the same way?
I believe it should and perhaps in a very reasonable time it will.

I do not know whether I
caught the remarks of the minister aright, but I understood him to be expressing satisfaction with the work of the inspection staff in Nova Scotia.
Yes.

I want to say in all sincerity *that if the minister thinks the inspection of fruit in Nova Scotia as carried on by his department is or has been satisfactory, he is making a very great mistake. I have discussed this matter a great deal lately with fruit growers in Nova Scotia. Many of the troubles of the fruit industry there are due to the incompleteness and inefficiency of the fruit inspection. Of course when I say that the packing and grading of apples in Nova Scotia are not what they should be, I know I am to some extent reflecting upon the packers and shippers themselves, but at the same time that is no excuse for the unevenness, lack of uniformity, of the inspection of fruit in that province. During the past season there was a very heavy crop, between two and three million barrels being grown in Nova Scotia, most of which were of course exported to Great Britain; and in conversation with buyers of apples I have been struck with the necessity that exists for improvement in the inspection of fruit in that province. I should like the minister to take this matter very seriously into consideration. This is perhaps the only time in the last two or three years that I have spoken about inspection, because what is called one hundred per cent inspection was put into force only in the fall of 1930 and the fruit growers and shippers in Nova Scotia have been disposed to give the system a fair trial to see whether it would work out. But members of the committee will realize that there has been a great change in the system since compulsory inspection was adopted. Before 1930 prosecutions were possible; penalties were imposed upon fruit growers and packers who did not comply with 
the grading regulations. But under the system under which all fruit for export must receive an inspection certificate, the mere granting of the certificate is prima facie evidence and, I think, conclusive proof, that the apples are properly packed, and if I am correctly informed no prosecutions take place at the present time because the inspectors are not supposed to pass the fruit unless it is packed up to standard. There is no question that there has been passed by inspectors a great deal of fruit which does not comply with the grading regulations. If the minister thinks, as his remarks would indicate, that the inspection has resulted in the fruit all being packed up to standard in that province, he is very much mistaken. I feel constrained to express myself as forcibly as I can upon this subject. The easy thing to do would be to say that we are doing very well in the packing of our fruit in Nova Scotia, and the majority of the fruit packers are doing very well, but there is a minority in that province that are not complying with the law. Some of them are not trying to comply with the law, and some of them, due to the great pressure of work during the past heavy season, did not comply with the law, putting, for example, 800 barrels of apples over a grader in a day when 400 barrels should be the limit, or a warehouse handling 200,000 barrels of apples in a season when it ought to try to handle only 100,000 barrels. These conditions lead to even the most honest warehouse foremen and managers turning out packs of fruit which are below grade. I woidd ask the Minister of Agriculture with the greatest possible earnestness to consider very carefully the improvement, by any method that his fruit branch may advise, of the inspection services at least in Nova Scotia.

I appreciate very
much the fact that the hon. member who has just spoken comes from a fruit growing and, in particular, an apple growing district. One thing that brought the matter to my attention was a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture in Nova Scotia on his return from the United Kingdom in February. While he did not expressly go into the question of the pack, anybody reading that speech and following it closely could not fail to realize the great regret he had that our apples as opened up on the British market had not been better graded and packed. It may be that I should have gone to the minister with this complaint before, but I must say that it was never borne in upon me as it was during the last two or three weeks, when I discussed the matter with a great many growers and shippers in Nova Scotia. There is a feeling on the part of the people engaged in the business there that they want a stern, rigid and thorough inspection of apples, and that they did not have it during the past season. In saying that I am not attacking all the inspectors; many of them have been doing the best they could; the trouble may be, as the minister says, due to the great size of the crop. But provision must be made for these heavy crops in future and more attention given to inspection by the department. *

I appreciate very
much the fact that this desire for a rigid inspection is evidenced by the fruit growers of Nova Scotia, because it is a very healthy sign. On the other hand I am still at a loss to understand, having regard to the hundred per cent effort on the part of the province and the federal department of agriculture to work in cooperation, why the Minister of Agriculture for the province has not communicated with the federal department with a view to planning a more rigid inspection. Doubtless however he will do so in the near future so that every preparation may be made to remedy any weakness in the inspection service.

I thank the minister. Now I should like to know whether there are inspectors stationed at the public markets to check the classification of fruits and vegetables and, if so, whether the minister was able to appoint citizens of the province of Quebec able to speak both languages. I understand that last year there were many

cases of, I will not say, the abuse of power, but where the rules and regulations were drastically applied by inspectors who could not explain themselves in the French language.
I made complaints, not because I have any prejudice against any citizens of this country but because it was a case of public necessity. Let me give an illustration. An inspector is stationed at the Bonsecours market in Montreal, and he checks up a farmer who has not classified his potatoes properly. The inspector speaks only English and the farmer speaks only French. The farmer may think the inspector is talking about the weather instead of about potatoes. I am only speaking from the practical point of view, and I should like to know if the minister can tell me that this year the inspectors will be able to make themselves understood in both languages in regard to this classification of fruit and vegetables, of which I am in favour so long as it is carried on in a spirit of cooperation.

I have a very full
appreciation of the importance of inspectors engaged in this work, in which they have to give reasons for their actions, being able to express themselves clearly in either English or French. As I said before, the appointments are made by the civil service commission, though sometimes we have to send additional inspectors to cooperate with and assist the bilingual inspectors at certain points. In this connection every effort is made to see that the inspector will be able to make himself understood in both languages. Should there be any criticism in this connection, though the appointments are made through the civil service commission, I should be very glad to bring the matter to their attention and to do everything possible to correct the situation.

I am very grateful for these remarks by the minister. I should like to remind hon. members that if they had an inspector on the Toronto market who tried to talk with the farmers in French I am sure they would not endure that situation for very long, and I would not blame them. Last year, if I am not mistaken, the inspector in charge of the Bonsecours market in Montreal was a gentleman named Robinson.
He was the district inspector.

He was the one wiho applied the law; he was the one who had our farmers arrested and brought before the criminal courts for having forgotten to put cards on the bags of potatoes stating the grade of
the contents. I remember that I represented those farmers several times, sometimes half a dozen, sometimes more and sometimes less, and the penalty was $10 and costs for having forgotten to put their names and the grades on the bags of potatoes. I tried to induce the inspector in charge to have the cases postponed, but he absolutely refused to do so. The cases came before Hon. Amedee Monet, and I asked for a delay of one week so that I could confer with the Montreal minister, the Minister of Marine, who, may I say in passing, was kind enough to take up this matter and bring it to the attention of the ministry. The inspector in charge, however, absolutely refused to agree to a delay or postponement, because the offence was so great. I said to Judge Monet, " A moment ago a man accused of manslaughter was granted a postponement of fifteen days. I wonder if the chief inspector considers that the failure to attach a oard showing the grade is as serious an offence as that of manslaughter." lit was only after that remark to the judge that I obtained a postponement to enable me to communicate with the Minister of Agriculture, whom I know to be a gentleman and one who wishes to give justice to those to whom justice is due. I said to the Minister of Marine that I wanted him to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, because I was sure he would not allow such a condition to exist. What occurred? I remember on one occasion I met an inspector who was able to speak both languages, and I was told by him, " I would be ready to be lenient in a first offence but the chief inspector said, ' Let those Frenchmen pay their fines; that is all they deserve'." I should like to bring to the notice of the minister a matter of which he has pebhaps full knowledge, and that is in regard to the apple bearing trees especially of western and central Ontario. My information is that owing to the abnormal sub-zero weather of last winter about fifty per cent of the apple trees have been killed. Has the minister any information in regard to that? I want it to be thoroughly understood, Mr. Chairman, that in bringing this matter before the minister I do not blame the government for this destruction. The government gets blamed for very many things without that. I am mentioning the matter because I thought the minister might have some statement to make.
The government made no promises about the trees.

I am afraid it is all too true that the sub-zero weather on a number of successive days has been very injurious to the apple trees not only of western Ontario but of eastern Ontario. There are those who feel not only that this year's fruit crop will be very seriously affected, if not in some cases wiped out one hundred per cent, but that the apple trees themselves because of the particular time at which the sub-zero temperatures came, will be killed. But I think it is too early yet to make a statement such as that. Our people have investigated the bark of the trees to the cambium layer, and their investigations have shown them that in some instances it has almost been destroyed, that this layer adjoining the bark through which the sap passes is injured and the bark can be pulled off readily by the hand. But personally I think it is too early to make any estimate of the lasting damage that may have been done to the apple tree. Certainly, however, there has been very serious injury.

I suppose I may take it from the minister's remarks that he and his department are fully aware of the situation and have it under consideration, and that they will consider it in the light of how the interests of the apple growers may be affected.
Yes.

Would the minister care to say anything about the extent of the damage in Nova Scotia? I know that officers of the department are making a survey with a view to getting definite information.

There has also beer some injury in Nova Scotia, but as I stated of Ontario I do not think anyone is in a position yet to say definitely how far-reaching in quantity or lasting in damage the injury has been.

I should like some information with regard to the assistance given the various provinces in regard to seed. Last year or the year before I directed a question to the minister with regard to seed that was required in a certain part of my county, and at that time I think the minister stated that it was not within the province of his department to supply seed unless it was absolutely required, and at the request of the province. Was any such request made and was any such assistance given in cooperation with any provincial government?

When I stated that seed was furnished only at the request of the provincial government my reply had reference to commercial seed, so to speak. Under this item no assistance is given by way of supplying commercial seed to farmers in drought areas, or farmers who cannot purchase seed themselves; so far as I know this government never has supplied seed in that way to the farmers of any province. This vote is divided in several ways. A certain amount is given each province, to be used by the province, together with its own money, to assist in improving the seed in that province, for example. In the west they wish to use that subvention in order to get better seed in the drought area, which in the past was one of our best sources of supply for good seed. The provinces have felt that this is the most important work to be done with this money, and they have asked that the subvention to those provinces should be used to furnish a better and purer supply of seed for those areas. So we pay the freight on carload and less than carload lots of pure seed from the northern districts to assist the people in the south to get that seed at a lower cost. For example, after the harvest last fall, following a survey, all the pure Marquis and Reward seed that was available was kept on hand and, with the assistance of this subvention, was sent to the south. This is not done in connection with commercial seed, however. In the eastern provinces they feel that the best contribution we can make towards the

improvement of their seed is to use this money to assist in the purchase of small seed cleaning plants. I believe the division is much on a set basis. I hope I have made myself clear.
For what purpose is the grant of $17,010 given to the Canadian Seed Growers' Association? Is that a similar association to the horticultural council?

No, it has to be used in a different way The Canadian Registered Seed Growers' Association conduct the registering of the pure seed grain, grasses and so on, throughout the dominion. It is to assist them in carrying out that work that this money is used. It rebounds to the benefit of all farmers in all provinces of the dominion, and brings about a uniform standard. If a farmer in Quebec wishes to have a variety of pure registered seed from British Columbia, for instance, he knows the exact quality of seed he is getting. He would not know however if there were separate legislation in each province. Their work is along the line of the Canadian National Live Stock Records Association.
Mr. CASGRAIN'. They have a branch in the province of Quebec?
Yes, they operate in each province.
To what extent is the federal seed branch being utilized in the west, where so much seed is necessary in the drought stricken areas?
I am informed that . the whole staff has been placed at the services of the province to inspect all grain being shipped for seed.

In view of the fact that the chief of the branch is sitting in front of the minister I should like to know if there has been any difficulty in the finding of necessary seed of good quality to take care of the demands of the western provinces?
Yes, there has been, and especially in connection with seed oats.

The relief commission.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which some time ago was placed before his department, namely, that of ithe sealing of seed oats shipped out of our province. For a number of years we have been shipping under seal seed oats to the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick. This seal was affixed by an official of the department. A few years ago the Department of Agriculture compelled our farmers to put their oats up in this manner, and- required the sealing of the sacks. For some reason this year they have been refused the privilege of having their sacks sealed and have had to ship out their grain with the sacks unsealed to the same people they have been shipping to in former years. This has created some suspicion in the minds of the farmers who have been buying seed for a great many years, and our business men find it hard to do business in the way they formerly did. I should like to know from the minister what pressure was brought to bear on the department to change this practice and withdraw from our farmers the privilege of having their seed grain sealed in sacks as formerly.

Formerly, when it
was necessary to seal the sack, that was an assurance to those who were buying the seed that the grain in that sack was from a seed crop that had been field inspected and designated as pure as to variety. I believe that due to pressure from farmers and perhaps some of the seed houses in Prince Edward Island, and the enthusiasm of one of our seed inspectors in that locality, it was felt that the community could perhaps best be served by sealing what looked to be and was clean commercial seed, but without any guarantee as to the variety. They wished that to be sealed, and with a certificate given, I believe. Many people thought it meant that it was practically the same as registered seed.

So far as pressure being brought to bear on the government to make the change is concerned, as soon as this matter was brought to my attention-I cannot say how it was brought to my attention-1 thought that it was not to the advantage of the farmers in Prince Edward Island, who have a decided advantage in being more or less isolated as they are, and I thought it would be a very simple thing for them to develop a supply of perhaps one hundred per cent pure seed that no other province could. Because of that I myself took the responsibility of doing away with sealing and of giving a certificate for commercial grain that was clean but whose purity we could not certify without growing it, and instead to give a certificate under seal only for pure field inspected grain. Here again I must reiterate that the farmers of Prince Edward Island have a very great advantage and opportunity, and I am sure that they will give full support to the policy of endeavouring to develop their registered seed grain almost one hundred per cent.

It is quite true that they have developed to a great extent the growing of pure seed and that they have followed tlhe field inspection service very closely. There is a large quantity of field inspected grain which is ready for shipment every year. But this was another matter apart altogether from the field inspected grain. It was a privilege that the farmers had when they brought in Banner oats, even if they could not certify that it was field inspected. The practice of affixing the seal was approved by the dealers. I would ask the minister if there have been any complaints from the receivers of this grain in the different provinces, that it was not true -to its name, or why was the practice discontinued?

I do not recall
whether or not there were any complaints from the receivers of the grain, but the information given to me when the matter first came to my attention was that Prince Edward Island had shipped in the amount of registered pure seed grain that they were growing, that they had not as high a percentage of pure registered grain as they had had before this practice crept in. The hon. member states that a farmer brings in a bag of clean Banner oats. We feel quite certain that in a great many cases they were not Banner oats although they were sealed as Banner oats, and because there was no assurance that the farmer was getting what he thought he was getting, and that Prince Edward Island

Mr. Chairman, at the session of parliament which was called to ratify the treaty resulting from the Imperial Economic Conference agreements, the government boasted and took credit for all the advantages which we would derive from such a treaty with Great Britain. We were told that the government, by granting a preference to Great Britain on chemical fertilizers imported into Canada, was rendering a very great service to the farming class. We protested at the time because the tariff was also being increased on chemical fertilizers imported from the United States. I simply wish to give to the house the list for the fiscal year 1933 of the products imported from the United States and the United Kingdom. As you may note, in most cases, the British preference granted on the various ingredients Which enter into the composition of chemical fertilizers served absolutely no purpose, because none were imported from Great Britain.
Let us take, for instance bone dust, charred bone and bone ash. We imported from the United States 26,437 cwts. of this ingredient and from the United Kingdom, 4,352 cwts. We imported from the United States 631,385 cwts. of phosphate rock while none were imported from the United Kingdom. We imported from the United States 1,640 cwts. of kainite or German potash salts and German mineral potash, while none came from the United Kingdom. We imported from the United States 347 cwts. of cyanamide of lime or lime nitrogen, while none was imported from Great Britain. We imported from the United States 6,413 cwts. of muriate of potash, While none was imported from Great Britain. Take as another instance, nitrate of soda. We imported from the United States 282,079 cwts. while we only imported from the United Kingdom 103 cwts.
I have a longer list; however, I shall dispense from reading it to the house. I simply wish to point out the fact that the Imperial Economic Conference agreements have been of no benefit to us so far as chemical fertilizers, unless it be an increase in their prices, because we increased the duty on the ingredients imported from the United States and, in most cases, all these ingredients are imported from that country.

I understood the hon. member to say that a tariff has been
placed on the ingredients, imported from the United States and other countries, which are used in this country to make fertilizer. My information is that no duty has been placed on such ingredients.
What about mixed fertilizer?
Yes, but not on the ingredients used to make fertilizer.
There are many ingredients that are not imported.
Is the hon. member asking how many ingredients are imported?
I know; that was what I stated in my remarks, which were based on an answer given by the government in the house.
That is supposed to be good, but sometimes they miss the mark.

I do not wish, sir, to detain the house; however, the agricultural situation is most deplorable at present. Glancing over the agricultural appropriations during the years this government has been in office, I note with regret that they show a decrease of more than $3,292,658.12. Taking into consideration the years of hardship through which we are passing, it strikes me that we should not have decreased but rather increased subsidies for the Department of Agriculture. Thus, in 1931, we find a decrease of about $375,000; in 1932, an increase of $414,000; in 1933, a decrease of more than $2,000,000, and in 1934 a decrease of nearly $391,000, while in 1935 in the estimates under consideration, we note a further decrease of more than $850,000.
I am aware that it may be a difficult task for the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) to convince his leader that large votes are necessary to carry on the work of his department; however, such a large decrease in the course of five years is altogether uncalled for, especially at a time when a back to the land movement is advocated.

As the hon. mem-,
ber has stated, there has been a very considerable reduction in the estimates for this department, but it has been made possible to a great extent by reorganization and the

reduction of expenses and not by any depreciation in services. On top of that there have been formulated policies that have given to the farmers, to a considerable degree, benefits which previously they had not enjoyed, particularly with respect to live stock. But in the reduction of the estimates, the test we have always kept before us has been that it should not mean a reduction in services which would in any way have a depressing or an injurious effect on the farmers or their agriculture.
Then the minister approves of this very considerable reduction in his own estimates.
Yes.
I am glad to hear that.

I stated on a previous occasion that the standard for these estimates was that there should not be any reduction in services that would materially affect in a damaging way the farmers. Let us take the item under discussion. The hon. member for Melville has stated what the reduction has been in the last three years. Another item of decrease in this particular vote is, as the hon. member knows, that due to the succession of crop failures in western Canada, there has been a considerable decrease in the demand for services for grain inspection which was perhaps one of the greatest services in agriculture in the western provinces prior to the crop failures. Similarly in different parts of the dominion there has been a decrease in the demand for inspectional services. On top of that, as I stated somewhat earlier in the evening, we have made very considerable reductions in travelling expenses and by doing our own laboratory work for the inspection of fertilizer, feeds and so on, by taking over a building that had formerly been occupied by the national research council. I have no hesitation in saying that with this decrease in the vote the services that are given to the farmers or to agriculture are still very efficient.

My hon. friend has
saved the situation by now claiming that there has been no material reduction. I like that term much better; it was the one he used last year. That is a very safe, flexible term to use and the hon. gentleman can get by with it; but I do not like the statement that there is no reduction in services, because nobody accepts it.

While on
this item would the minister give us some information in regard to crested wheat grass? A couple of years ago in the agriculture committee he told us something that to me was rather interesting with regard to that grass. I saw a small patch of it growing last summer in a very dry district in my constituency and it appeared to me that it was quite successful there. Has the minister any information to give in that regard?

I think it is a safe statement to make that the hope for crested wheat grass and what it will accomplish is even greater than I stated to the committee a year ago, and I recall that in that statement fMr.' Casgrain.]
I	was quite enthusiastic. As the hon. member has indicated, especially in districts where there is a great lack of moisture, crested wheat grass is particularly suitable. Even in our Manyberries station, where there is a considerable area that had been abandoned by farmers on account of lack of moisture, experiments have been made with crested wheat grass, brome, sweet clover, western rye grass and some other grasses, comparing them as to the growth they make with a limited amount of moisture. In those experiments crested wheat grass showed itself much superior to the other grasses. One noticeable thing about these iplots was that in the crested wheat grass plot there were practically no weeds; its tendency to absorb the moisture was so great that there was not sufficient moisture left for the weeds to make headway. Another advantage of this grass is that it is a cool weather grass as well as a dry season grass; when the snow goes off in the spring it is as green as it is perhaps at any time of the year. Also it is a very palatable grass, and it has a high yield of seed. In the fall when the cool weather comes on it seems to take new life, because it is particularly adaptable to cool weather and remains green and maintains a fine growth until covered by snow. Another important characteristic that it has, especially important in very dry areas, is that when even western rye grass will not withstand the drought and can be easily knocked out by the roots, and brome grass withers and often dies, the crested wheat grass seems to become dormant, but responds to the very slightest degree of moisture. One of the hardest tests that crested wheat grass has experienced was in a seeding that took place on the lawn of Professor Harrington in Saskatoon. He had a cement sidewalk running through his lawn, both sides of which were seeded with crested wheat grass, particularly the fairway strain, which is one of our most likely strains for fairways on golf courses and for laying down sod in western Canada. It is a strain that is rich in foliage and spreads more than some of the other strains of crested wheat grass. One side was watered and protected, on the other side the children of Professor Harrington and his neighbours played and it became almost like a pavement. Then towards the middle of August it also was watered and protected, and it responded very quickly, and before the winter set in showed an excellent growth.
It has always been realized by those interested in diversified farming, particularly in the west, that the need was for a domestic

Supply-Agriculture-Fruit
grass. We believe that in almost every respect crested wheat grass will meet that need, not only in the dry areas, but it also stands up well in the northern areas. At the Indian Head forestry station some years ago two pounds I believe were seeded, very sparsely, and there were threshed from this patch 1,320 pounds of seed. That also is another very important characterictic of this grass, its high yield. Another most important feature is that you can allow the seed of crested wheat grass to mature and then cut and thresh it and the stalks of the grass still remain green and palatable, unlike western rye and other grasses of that nature which if allowed to ripen in the least become woody and dusty and not palatable.

As far as the experiments
have gone would the minister advise using it with a nurse crop or by itself?

It depends a good
deal upon the locality. I would say that while of course any grass does better if seeded with a nurse crop, in the locality where the home of the hon. member for Lisgar is it would not be necessary in a normal season to use a nurse crop with crested wheat grass. It germinates very readily; it has a quick growth and it does not need to be seeded to any great depth; the shallower it is seeded the better. In that district in the normal season I would say that a nurse crop is not at all necessary. Sow it early.

I thank the minister for that explanation, because I have been greatly interested in crested wheat grass. I think it was two years ago I made inquiry and found the seed was not available. I wonder if it is available at the present time.

Commercial quality seed is available in considerable quantities. There comes to my mind a gentleman who has made a fine success of growing this grass in Alberta, Mr. Moore of Bindloss. I purchased considerable seed from him last year for my own farm, and it was very satisfactory as was also the price. A selected strain like the fairway strain is not so plentiful; there is a limited supply, and the present price is fifty cents a pound.
I think it can be got at the university at Saskatoon.

Will the department
have any seed of that grass for sale?

The department is
always a source of inquiry for grass seed. It has a list of those who have grasses for sale.
I can give that information, or if the hon. member would have his correspondent write to the central experimental farm at Ottawa they would put him in touch with anyone who wanted the grass. If he himself knows anyone who has a supply for sale and will give that information to the central experimental farm I believe there is a big demand for it this year.

I had a note to ask
about this crested wheat grass and how much seed was available. It seems to me that on an occasion such as this we should avail ourselves of the opportunity to discuss with the minister just such things as this. Another prominent and I think useful seed has been developed, although it is only in its infancy as yet. I had the honour and privilege, I may say, yesterday or the day before of discussing this with the minister, and it just goes to show what you can do when you have a minister in charge of a department with the work of which he is very familiar. On his own farm to-day the minister has available a quantity of seed oats, and I think it would be interesting to have him tell us about these oats. They are a new or at least an outstanding variety of the hulless oat known as the Laurel, and in the discussion I had with the minister he was kind enough to promise to deliver some of these oats to my farm. It would be interesting to many of us if the minister would say a few words with regard to this variety, as to how well adapted it is for use as feed and for what other purposes it may be used.

If I had known the hon. member was going to say this I think I would have quoted him a lower price on the oats. Work has been carried on for a number of years in different countries, including the United Kingdom, the United States and particularly in Canada, in the development of the hulless oat. The difficulty has been in getting a strong enough straw and in getting an oat that would give a sufficiently high yield. It is believed now that these difficulties have been pretty well met by the oat mentioned by my hon. friend, the Laurel variety of hulless oat. It is particularly strong in the straw and yet not too coarse to be used for green feed for horses, cattle and calves. Since it is a hulless oat it makes better feed, especially for cattle, than oats having the hulls on, and those who are engaged in live stock farming will realize the wastage in feeding oats with hulls without crushing them, particularly in regard to cattle. That is one of the chief advantages
Supply-Agriculture-Fruit

of hulless oats as a green feed. Horses are particularly fond of it, and our experience has been that they do better on it than on other forms of green feed we have used. The yield is not quite as high as in the case of such oats as Gopher, Banner and Victory, yet it is quite a high yield; with a normal crop it runs to fifty, sixty or perhaps seventy bushels per acre, and a measured bushel of a good sample of hulless oats should weigh in the neighbourhood of fifty pounds. It is an early maturing variety and, contrary to what one would expect, the oats cling to the straw when it is quite ripe.
May I just ask a question suggested by my good friend from Vancouver Centre. He would like the minister to tell us if the new variety is good for oatmeal.

I am glad that question has come up. One of the great advantages of the hulless oat is that it has been made use of for some time by homesteaders. It is particularly adapted to the making of porridge by soaking without even having it ground. It is grown by homesteaders, pioneers in outlying districts, because of that quality, and for the reason that it has no hulls it is very suitable for feeding young pigs.
I notice that part of this vote is for grants to seed fairs. Can the minister tell us what seed fairs receive these grants, and how much they receive?

Some of this money goes to each province for seed fairs. I am sorry we have not a list of the seed fairs receiving grants. I should be glad to send that list to my hon. friend, showing the grants paid in all the provinces or just in the province of Saskatchewan, if that would satisfy the hon. gentleman.

Item agreed to.
Live stock, including assistance to fairs and exhibitions, $1,518,302.
Will the minister explain the reason for the decrease in this item?

In the reorganization of this branch a saving of something like $300,000 has been made chiefly by combining six branches into three and consolidating the services so that officials have a freer hand to do work which is not so closely defined as hitherto has been the case. There has been practically no reduction of service except in connection with cow testing, which is different from R.O.P. testing. The

provinces agreed that they should undertake cow testing, which gave us an opportunity to make further efforts in connection with R.O.P. testing. We have had many comments to the effect that this reorganization has improved the services given.
Has there been any decrease in the amount allotted to the province of Quebec for fairs and exhibitions due to the reduction in the item?
No, the grant is the same as it was last year.
How much does the province of Quebec receive under this vote for fairs?
A very large share in comparison with the other provinces. I have not the figures before me.
Has the minister any idea how much is paid out of this vote for exhibitions and fairs in the province of Quebec?
I have not the total, but I can get the amount for each fair and give it to the hon. member.
I notice this item includes assistance to fairs and exhibitions. This is rather a large item, and I wonder if the minister could tell us just how this money is to be spent.

The vote is made up as follows:
Field services	$540,084
Market services	 256,684
Poultry services	 266,797
General services	 175,237
Exhibitions	 279,500

At this point would the minister give the committee some information with regard to the regional fairs that were brought into existence by the minister during his administration, particularly as to how they were received?

We tried out the
policy of regional fairs at first by having one fair in each province and the results were satisfactory. The following year we allotted the grant to a different fair in each province. The satisfaction expressed especially by farmers was such that last year we offered regional grants to all so-called class B fairs except in cases where such interfered with provincial plans. As I said before the farmers felt that the fairs had had a very good effect in stimulating people other than professional show people to exhibit.

Supply-Agriculture-Live Stock

Is it the intention of
the department to increase the regional fairs this year or to maintain or curtail them?
It is not the intention of the department to curtail them but on the whole to leave them as they were last year.
With the same grant?

Yes. In one or
two isolated districts it may be possible that there may be additional regional fairs.
I should like to know if there will be any change this year in the grants for class B fairs in Saskatchewan?
No.
How many of these regional fairs are there in Alberta?

Would the minister
enumerate the fairs, and tell us where they are held?

They are as follows:

Manitoba:

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an extract from the March 12th issue of the publication L'Action Catholique. My translation is as follows:
One or our readers sent us a copy of the following letter which he received from one of the government services:
"February 25, 1934.
Dear Sir:
We have received your letter of the 13th instant, asking for a French copy of our report.
We regret to inform you that owing to the expense and lack of funds we no longer publish Our report in French.
Yours truly,
Canadian National Live Stock Records.
W. Brant,
Accountant."
Would the minister give an explanation in this matter?

The Canadian
National Live Stock Records is not part of the federal Department of Agriculture. Originally each breeding association had its own registration. It was felt after some time that by a combination of their efforts they could give a cheaper and better service. With that in mind practically all the breeders have so combined. The Holstein breeders are not included; they continue to operate their own bureau and have their own registration office. The letter to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Kamouraska does not apply to the Department of Agriculture.
Do they not receive a grant?

May I add a word? If the hon. member would look at a later edition of the same publication he would see therein a letter addressed by Mr. Charles Fremont confirming my colleague's statement, pointing out that the federal government had nothing whatsoever to do with their activities, and stating further that the only reason for not issuing any more French copies was that they had no funds.

I do not find fault with that. But if the Canadian National Live Stock Records Association is receiving an increased grant from the government they may be in a position to have the French copy published. However I have no criticism to offer.

I should be glad to discuss this matter with the Canadian National Live Stock Records Association. I know that the hon. member who has just spoken is deeply interested in agriculture and has special influence with some of the breeders' associations of the province of Quebec which would benefit from printing the publications in the French language. I should hope that between the two of us, even with their depleted finances, it might be possible to have the copies printed in French, because I heartily agree that the publication would be beneficial to the French farmers who, in recent years, particularly, have shown great interest in the improvement of their live stock.
Progress reported.

I could not see for the life of me why he could not give the amount of the line of credit that the government had guaranteed Mr. McFarland in connection with the handling of his wheat activities on the Winnipeg grain exchange. The information will be quite incomplete if that item is left out. We want the total. That is what I am after. I want to be able to say: The government spent $110,000,000 for relief and two or three hundred million, whatever it is, under the same act, under the guise of relief. The excuse for not giving information regarding the guarantee is that it would hurt the price of wheat. Of course I would not want to hurt the price of wheat. It is bad enough now. But what possible effect can disclosing the amount of this guar-

antee have on the price of wheat? What was the line of credit that was given up to the end of the last grain year, the first of August say? Was it the same all through? How much of it was used? I am not wanting to get at the amount of wheat held by Mr. McFarland. That is not the point at all. We pretty nearly know that, and it does not make any difference.
I want to assure the Prime Minister that I have often used this guarantee, in speaking to the people of the west, as an indication that the government was desirous of helping the farmer, although I had some grave doubts as to its advantage, for the simple reason that to the extent it kept up the price and kept our price out of line with competing countries, to that extent we frequently lost sales, because when your price is out of line with competing countries then they will get the sales. In looking for something this government has done I have used that guarantee both out in the west and in this house and said that the government should be given some credit for desiring at least to improve conditions. Why then cannot we be given the amount and extent of this guarantee? Other guarantees have been given by other governments and there has been no hesitation in stating the amounts. Our own government in Saskatchewan as already indicated, guaranteed a line of credit for the co-operative elevators and published the amount freely. From Washington from month to month we got at least the amount of the guarantees that were made a few years ago for a similar purpose. Why should that information be concealed here? I think what I am urging is as much in the interests of the government as of anybody else. As I say, I have used this guarantee as one of the few things which this government has done on behalf of the grain market. Even if it did not affect the price much if any, their intentions were good. Why this concealment? Why this star chamber method of doing business? Why this hole-in-the-corner method in regard to finance?
The government has taken the ground that we should cultivate better ethics in business. The Prime Minister's colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in discussing the question before the committee on mass buying and in his Toronto speech, took the ground that the chain stores and the mail order houses had departed from what was the proper thing in business ethics. But

Communters Canada-United States
what are we to say of this kind of business ethics, using the credit of the country on behalf of a guarantee for promoting better marketing, and doing it in this clandestine manner? Is that good business ethics? Would it be in anybody else but the government? Would it be good business ethics for a private member of this house not to report candidly in his private business affairs to the shareholders or the people whose money was involved? I plead with the Prime Minister. Jt is not his usual practice to do business in a slithery way like this, and it is not the teaching and preaching of the government. It is not what they are out to inculcate in the minds of the people of Canada through the Stevens committee. They are practically merely saying: Do not do as I do, but do as I say. I want to know if it is out of order to press too hard for this information simply because the matter has been before the banking committee. Actually the matter was settled in the banking committee although that committee has not yet formally reported to the house. It was decided in the committee not to ask for the information, but having the Prime Minister of Canada now before us I plead with him to give us this information I am asking for. It is for himself to decide, but if he does not tell us I am afraid his blood will have to be on his own head; it will not be my fault because I have been asking for the information for several years.
